summary.text:
Aberdeen City Council's Treasury Management Policy 2026/27 to 2028/29 (CORS/26/002, doc 176276) went to Council on 4 February 2026 as a six-page covering report seeking approval of a forward policy statement. Read alongside are its Appendix 1 (doc 176277, the eighteen-page policy limits document tabled at the same meeting) and the previous substantive treasury paper, the mid-year review to Council on 10 December 2025 (CORS/25/277, doc 176223). The covering report itself carries no quantified treasury exposure at all — its own §3.7 says 'there are no key changes' within either the Borrowing or Investment Policies, and §3.21 defers the Prudential Indicators 2026/27 to 2030/31 to a separate budget paper on 4 March 2026. Appendix 1 is a limits document (fixed 30-100%, variable 0-30%; five maturity buckets with upper/lower percentages; £250m/£100m/£10m caps on non-deposit permitted investments; counterparty list unchanged since 16 April 2025) and its only quantified position is a single sentence at §5.2: 'Approximately 69% of the Council's long-term borrowing is long-term fixed rate PWLB loans.'

The 69% claim is the paper's only test. Our PWLB file at 4 February 2026 returns £839,433,564 across 63 MATURITY loans at a weighted 3.9569%. If PWLB is 69% of long-term borrowing, total long-term is roughly £1,216.6m and the non-PWLB long-term component is roughly £377m. Aberdeen publicly issued a £370m 30-year RPI Bond in 2016 (referenced obliquely by §5.1 of the covering report and by §3.11 of the mid-year); £370m + £839.4m = £1,209.4m and £839.4m / £1,209.4m = 69.4%, consistent with the paper's 'approximately 69%' to a rounding. Soft cross-check for the internal record only — the paper prints neither the total nor the Bond principal, so this tie is not being raised externally as a reconciliation.

The substantive numbers all sit in the mid-year. §3.4 records four new long-term PWLB loans totalling £70m drawn earlier in 2025/26 at an average 4.45% and average life of 5 years, with 'substantial long-term borrowing was planned for this financial year, but market conditions have not been favourable' as the reason more was not taken. §3.5 records c£329m of temporary inter-authority borrowing at an average 4.74%. That side-by-side placement is the paper's own tension: the cheaper money is the kind Aberdeen has said it struggled to place enough of, and the more expensive is what carries the current cash-flow position. §3.6 adds £11.1m of temporary borrowing from the North-East of Scotland Pension Fund's excess cash. Investments are c£34m of temporary balances at 4.05% (§3.7), plus £30m of Common Good in a Fidelity Multi-Asset Income fund (£5.37m cumulative interest since 2021, average 4.21% — a since-inception figure, not an in-year yield). Moody's A2 stable was confirmed 9 October 2025 (§3.12).

Balance-sheet identity is not testable from any of the three papers — no CFR, no external-borrowing figure and no other-long-term-liabilities figure is printed anywhere. Recorded as missing, not derived. The maturity profile is likewise not printed; our own file shows the shape (58% of the £819m live PWLB balance at 25y+ at a weighted 3.69%; the remaining 42% split across shorter buckets at 3.58-4.58%), and every bucket sits well inside the Appendix 1 §5.2 caps. A loan-book reconciliation on principal, count or weighted rate is not attempted because the paper prints none of those figures.

Rate move since the paper's reference dates: today's 5-year PWLB certainty at 5.34% is ~89bp above the 4.45% average the mid-year records for the four loans drawn earlier in 2025/26; today's 1-year certainty at 4.95% is ~21bp above the 4.74% the mid-year records for the c£329m of temporary LA borrowing at that time. Both landscapes have moved further against a 'wait for a better window' judgement since December, rather than back toward it. This is the frame the email uses.

Officer contact: Lesley Fullerton, Finance Operations Manager (lfullerton@aberdeencity.gov.uk, 01224 067157) — verbatim from the covering report contact block, p.6. She is the report author. The statutory finance officer under Section 95 of the Local Government (Scotland) Act 1973 is Jonathan Belford, Chief Officer - Finance (front sheet, p.1; Appendix 1 §3.2). Belford's email is NOT printed in any of the three papers, so he is not on the recipient line. Neil Stewart, Treasury Management Officer (nstewart@aberdeencity.gov.uk), authored the mid-year and is cc'd since most of what the email discusses sits in his paper. Email drafted; no forward committee date is published for the next treasury paper.

officer.subject: The mid-year's £329m at 4.74% next to £70m at 4.45% — and where the market has gone since
officer.body:
Hi Lesley,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the Treasury Management Policy tabled at Council on 4 February, read alongside its Appendix 1 and the mid-year that went to Council on 10 December. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. The 4 February policy is deliberately a limits paper and asserts 'no significant changes' from the previous cycle; this is offered in that spirit rather than as a critique.

The thing that stands out is a tension the mid-year sets out plainly in adjacent paragraphs. Paragraph 3.4 records four new long-term PWLB loans totalling £70m drawn earlier in 2025/26 at an average 4.45% and an average life of five years, with 'substantial long-term borrowing was planned for this financial year, but market conditions have not been favourable' as the reason more was not taken. Paragraph 3.5 records roughly £329m of temporary inter-authority borrowing at an average 4.74% — a rate 29 basis points above the new-PWLB average, on more than four times the amount. The cheaper money is the kind you have said the market didn't let you place enough of; the more expensive is what is carrying the current cash flow position.

Where the market has gone since December is the harder side of the same question. Today's 5-year PWLB certainty rate is 5.34% — about 89 basis points above the 4.45% average the mid-year records for the loans drawn earlier in 2025/26. Today's 1-year certainty rate is 4.95% — about 21 basis points above the 4.74% the mid-year records for the temporary LA borrowing. So the 'wait for a better window' judgement in December has been outrun on both sides rather than vindicated. Both remain live in the sense the mid-year describes — you remain open to further long-term borrowing, and the LA short-term market remains available — but the arithmetic on both has moved against the December position, not back toward it.

One piece of context on the wider book. Our PWLB file for Aberdeen City at the 4 February date holds 63 loans totalling roughly £839m at a weighted 3.96%, all MATURITY. About 58% of the current live balance sits in the 25-year-and-over bucket at a weighted 3.69%, which is what pulls the whole-book rate below four per cent. The Appendix 1 caps at §5.2 leave a lot of room on every bucket — the paper's real question is not headroom under the limits but where to place the next term-out decision on the yield curve.

The pages that go with all this: today's rates at both fixings and the whole curve are at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard; the monthly sector breakdown at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity shows what everyone else is drawing (July 2026 was £368m across 33 loans from 19 borrowers, average 5.02%); and pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis prices any PWLB position daily against the DMO's repayment curve. We hold PWLB only — the 2016 Bond issuance and the LA short-term book both sit outside our file by design, so we're not implying the PWLB file is the whole debt.

Free accounts for the whole team, and our 115 courses — officers and members, SONIA through to the Prudential Code — are free to local authorities until the end of September. Three that fit what the mid-year is describing: Intra-LA borrowing and lending markets (where the £329m sits), PWLB rates and the certainty discount, and Cost of carry and internal borrowing.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
